headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress create default data-leak and prompt-injection risks; no documented isolation between CrewAI and Semantic Kernel.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI reads and writes the host working directory and uses stdin/stdout, while Semantic Kernel can read/write application-defined files and call MCP/OpenAPI tools. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if one agent consumes the other's files or tool outputs. The pair lacks documented provenance tracking, so interaction risk is real but not clearly high.
conditions: IF CrewAI writes attacker-controlled text into a shared file that Semantic Kernel later parses as instructions
IF Semantic Kernel exposes MCP or plugin output that CrewAI treats as trusted prompt content
mitigations: Separate their working directories
Add a strict file-format parser for any cross-agent handoff
Prefix all inter-agent content with immutable provenance metadata
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from files
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware message routing

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, with broad network egress and host filesystem access; Semantic Kernel handles application context plus model-provider and plugin credentials, also with broad egress. If they share a workspace or memory store, either can expose the other's sensitive context to external model providers or tools. The blast radius includes secrets and work products, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or memory store
IF either agent forwards file contents or context to a third-party model provider or plugin
mitigations: Use separate credentials for each agent
Keep secrets out of shared files
Restrict each agent to a distinct workspace
Review outbound tool endpoints before execution
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files and make broad network calls, and both support multiple instances. CrewAI writes the host working directory; Semantic Kernel writes application-defined files and can coordinate via shared memory stores. Without explicit locking or namespace separation, concurrent writes can clobber shared artifacts or race on mutable state. The overlap is substantial but not clearly irreversible.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or memory store
IF either agent performs concurrent writes without an external lock
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable shared mutable state between instances
Check for stale artifacts before each run
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework with shared memory, and Semantic Kernel is a kernel-plus-plugins agent pattern. That makes it plausible for one agent's output to become the other's input without a verification step, especially when tool outputs are treated as authoritative. The pair can therefore propagate mistaken facts into downstream actions, but the profiles do not prove automatic action-taking.
conditions: IF CrewAI-generated text is fed into Semantic Kernel prompts without validation
IF Semantic Kernel executes plugin actions based on CrewAI outputs
mitigations: Insert a human review step for cross-agent outputs
Require schema validation on handoff messages
Log and diff all agent-to-agent transfers
Mark unverified outputs as non-authoritative
requires-engineering: add policy checks before tool execution

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and only indicate generic developer-passed crew data or application context, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. Because the pairwise compliance surface is underspecified, I cannot prove a breach pathway; the safer choice is low rather than none due to uncertainty around shared handling of secrets and context.
conditions: IF the operator routes regulated data through both agents under different retention or residency policies
IF one agent logs data longer than the other
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Compare retention settings before deployment
Document which agent stores which data class
Purge logs after test runs
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across both stacks
